o: 강연, 독서 모임, 어린이 프로그램을 연다

title: A History of Libraries
paras: Ever since people invented writing, they have wondered how to keep their records safe. Scattered records cannot be found when they are needed, and once lost they are hard to recover. So places arose where records could be gathered together, put in order, and protected. That is how libraries began.

Some of the oldest collections of records come from ancient Mesopotamia. People there pressed letters into wet clay tablets with the tip of a reed, then dried or baked the tablets to keep them. Clay was heavier and clumsier than paper, but when it was fired it actually grew harder, which allowed many tablets to survive for thousands of years.

In the seventh century BC, the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal gathered a large number of clay tablets in his capital, Nineveh. Besides government records, the collection included writings on omens, medicine, and literature. After the city fell, the tablets lay buried for a very long time until they were dug up in the modern era. Among them were parts of an ancient poem, the Epic of Gilgamesh.

The most famous library of the ancient world was the Library of Alexandria in Egypt. Around the third century BC, the Ptolemaic dynasty that ruled the city invited scholars there and worked hard to collect books from many lands. Most books at the time were scrolls of papyrus. Scholars copied, compared, and studied texts there, and the library became known as a great center of learning.

How the Library of Alexandria disappeared is still not clear. A popular story says that a single great fire destroyed everything, but historians disagree about what really happened. Many think that damage from war, shrinking support, and a slow decline over a long period all played a part. What is certain is that the library's name and its story have been passed down to this day.

Before printing, the only way to make more books was to copy them by hand. In the monasteries of medieval Europe, monks sat in writing rooms and copied books letter by letter. Making a single book could take months, so books were precious, and some libraries even chained their books to the desks so that none would go missing. Because copying by hand also introduced missing or mistaken words, scholars compared several copies with one another to recover the original text.

Around the same time, learning flourished in the Islamic world. In Baghdad, the capital of the Abbasid caliphs, there is said to have been a center of scholarship known as the House of Wisdom. Scholars there translated books from Greek and other languages into Arabic and studied them, and some of the knowledge preserved in this way later made its way back to Europe.

In the middle of the fifteenth century, Gutenberg introduced a printing press using metal type in Europe, and the world of books changed dramatically. Once many copies of the same book could be printed quickly, books became cheaper, and the number of people who owned books, and the number of libraries, grew steadily. Libraries began to shift from storerooms visited by a few toward places that many more people could use.

Korea, too, has a long tradition of treasuring books. In the year he came to the throne, King Jeongjo of Joseon founded the Kyujanggak inside the royal palace. It was not only a place to store royal books and records but also a place where young scholars gathered to read, study, and discuss policy. Many of the materials once collected there survive today and are still used in research.

In the nineteenth century, public libraries that anyone could use free of charge spread in many countries. As more people learned to read, the idea grew that even those who could not afford books should have a chance to learn. The American businessman Andrew Carnegie gave large sums of money that helped build a great many library buildings across the English-speaking world.

As collections grew, finding the right book became more important. Libraries gave books numbers by subject so that books in the same field would sit together on the shelves. They also wrote each book's details on small cards and filed them in drawers so that readers could search by title, author, or subject. For a long time, this card catalog was where every visit to the library began. Librarians made new cards for every book that arrived and filed them in the right place, and readers flipped through the drawers one card at a time to find a book's number before heading to the shelves.

Today, card catalogs have largely been replaced by computer searches. Readers can look through a library's collection from home and download e-books or research papers to read. In many places, old books and documents are also being photographed page by page and preserved as digital files.

That does not mean libraries matter less. Many of them do far more than lend books: they host talks, reading groups, and programs for children, and they have become places where people gather. Serving as a space open to everyone, where information is shared fairly, remains one of the most important jobs a library does.

From rooms stacked with clay tablets to a search box on a screen, libraries have changed enormously. Yet their purpose has stayed the same from the very beginning: to gather records, put them in order, and pass them on to the people who come next.
